text: From space, at night, Egypt is almost completely dark.
Except for one line.
More than a hundred million people, packed along a single river.
sub: More than 100 million people, packed along a single river.

text: This is how that line was drawn, and why it is now under pressure.
Egypt is bigger than France and Germany put together.
But about ninety-five percent of Egyptians live along the Nile, on roughly four percent of the land.
sub: But about 95% of Egyptians live along the Nile, on roughly 4% of the land.

text: The rest is the Sahara. Cairo gets less than three centimetres of rain in a whole year.
sub: The rest is the Sahara. Cairo gets less than 3 cm of rain in a whole year.

text: So about ninety-seven percent of Egypt's water comes from one river.
sub: So about 97% of Egypt's water comes from one river.

text: And along most of its length, the green strip it waters is narrow.
Near Qena, we measured it on a satellite image from 2025.
sub: Near Qena, we measured it on a 2025 satellite image.

text: At the narrowest point, the whole strip is just eight point four kilometres wide.
sub: At the narrowest point, the whole strip is just 8.4 km wide.

text: Fields, villages, roads, and the river itself. Sand on both sides.
For thousands of years, that strip was made by a flood.
Every summer, rain in the Ethiopian highlands swelled the Nile, and the river spilled over its banks.
When the water drew back, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud.
Ancient Egyptians called their country Kemet. The black land.
Then, in nineteen seventy, Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam.
sub: Then, in 1970, Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam.

text: Behind it grew Lake Nasser, one of the largest man-made lakes in the world.
It stretches about five hundred and fifty kilometres, from Egypt into Sudan.
sub: It stretches about 550 km, from Egypt into Sudan.

text: The dam ended the floods. It gave Egypt water all year round, and electricity.
But it also stopped the mud. More than ninety-eight percent of the river's sediment now settles in the lake.
sub: But it also stopped the mud. More than 98% of the river's sediment now settles in the lake.

text: Farmers downstream had to replace the river's mud with fertiliser. And the coast lost its supply of new land.
This is Rosetta, where one branch of the Nile meets the Mediterranean.
In nineteen seventy-two, the river mouth reached far out to sea, built up over centuries of Nile mud.
sub: In 1972, the river mouth reached far out to sea, built up over centuries of Nile mud.

text: Here is the same place in twenty twenty-five.
sub: Here is the same place in 2025.

text: The tip of the land has pulled back three point eight kilometres. We measured it on the two images.
sub: The tip of the land has pulled back 3.8 km. We measured it on the two images.

text: Without new mud, the sea kept eating the coast, until Egypt built a sea wall here in the early nineties.
sub: Without new mud, the sea kept eating the coast, until Egypt built a sea wall here in the early '90s.

text: Today, this coast is held in place by concrete, not by the river.
And much of the northern delta lies barely above sea level.
Meanwhile, the people kept coming.
Egypt had about twenty-seven million people in nineteen sixty. Today it has more than a hundred and nine million.
sub: Egypt had about 27 million people in 1960. Today it has more than 109 million.

text: Cairo alone has roughly twenty-five million. It is the largest city in Africa.
sub: Cairo alone has roughly 25 million. It is the largest city in Africa.

text: This is Cairo in nineteen eighty-four.
sub: This is Cairo in 1984.

text: And this is Cairo in twenty twenty-five.
sub: And this is Cairo in 2025.

text: New cities have spread into the sand on both sides. But Cairo has also grown over its own fields.
Comparing the two images, roughly one in four of the fields that were green here in nineteen eighty-four are now built over.
sub: Comparing the two images, roughly 1 in 4 of the fields that were green here in 1984 are now built over.

text: Most of it happened one building at a time, as villages and towns spread into the fields around them.
In a country with so little farmland, every field lost to concrete is hard to replace.
So Egypt is trying to move people out of the valley.
East of Cairo, this was empty sand in twenty fifteen.
sub: East of Cairo, this was empty sand in 2015.

text: Ten years later, it is a new capital city, with government ministries and the tallest building in Africa.
Whether millions of people will follow is still an open question.
Far to the south, the river is pushed into the desert too.
In wet years, Lake Nasser overflows into the Toshka depression, and lakes appear where there was only sand.
They first formed in nineteen ninety-eight, and they grow and shrink with the floods.
sub: They first formed in 1998, and they grow and shrink with the floods.

text: Next to them, new farms are now watered from the lake. Green circles, in one of the driest places on Earth.
From space, Egypt is still one bright line.
A line drawn by a river, held in place by a dam, and squeezed by more than a hundred million people.
